name: Kru Pidgin English / Liberian English
confidence_why: Nothing read states where word stress falls in Kru Pidgin English or what kind of prominence system it has: Singler 2004 describes Liberian Settler English, a different variety, and says only that the other Liberian Englishes are syllable-timed with every syllable of equal weight, and Singler 1981 adds only that negative auxiliaries carry high pitch, so the record stays undetermined.

catalog_quote: 2.2.2. Prosody (a) Stress-timing The prosody of LibSE sets it apart from all other Liberian varieties of English and, indeed, all other Liberian languages. All of the languages other than LibSE - including VLE at its most acrolectal – are strict syllable-timed languages. Essentially, every syllable gets equal weight and, consequently, vowel reduction rarely occurs. In contrast, LibSE is far less syllable-timed, hence more stress-timed. It seems appropriate to position the syllable-timed languages of Liberia at one pole, white northern American dialects of English at the opposite pole, and LibSE somewhere in between (cf. Thomas and Carter 2003). Certainly, there is far less vowel reduction in LibSE than in the white dialects of American English. [Singler 2004: 883] ... One of the differences between Liberian languages and American English is that the former are syllable-timed while the latter is stress-timed. In a syllable-timed language, each syllable is of approximately the same duration. [Singler 1981: 56] ... A distinguishing characteristic of all the negative auxiliaries is that they are pronounced with a raised pitch. Sometimes the pitch is a high level tone, and other times it is a rising tone, starting at a lower level and ending at a high pitch. In either case, the endpoint is raised. [Singler 1981: 44]

new_statements.rule_in_words: No source located gives a placement rule for word stress in Kru Pidgin English. The closest first-hand statement (Singler 2004, the main describer of KPE) is about rhythm class: every Liberian variety of English other than Liberian Settler English — i.e. Vernacular Liberian English and, by the chapter's own taxonomy, KPE — is strictly syllable-timed, every syllable carrying equal weight with little vowel reduction; Liberian Settler English is intermediate between that and stress-timed American English. Against this, Singler 1981 (Intro to Liberian English, pp. 29, 43) still refers to 'stressed' vs 'unstressed' syllables in Liberian English words at their English positions (blocking intervocalic lenition; burn vs teacher), and both 1981 (p. 45) and 1990 (pp. 209, 229) treat pitch/tone on negative auxiliaries as the salient prosodic feature. Hence: no stress-placement statement; rhythm described as syllable-timed; pitch used grammatically on negators.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: Liberian Settler English itself is 'far less syllable-timed, hence more stress-timed' (Singler 2004: 883); 'VLE at its most acrolectal' remains strictly syllable-timed. Singler 1981: 45 — all negative auxiliaries (not, don't, ain't, can't, never, no) carry raised pitch (high level or rising tone).
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is about the rhythm of connected speech across whole varieties (LibSE vs VLE/KPE vs Liberian Niger-Congo languages), not about citation-form word stress; no word-level stress placement is discussed for KPE anywhere opened.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog libe1240 'Kru Pidgin English' carries the alt. names Liberian English / Liberian Pidgin English and ISO lir 'Liberian English', and its only Glottolog descriptive ref is Singler's Liberian Settler English chapter — so Glottolog lumps Liberia's Englishes (Kru Pidgin English of the Klao/Grebo mariners, Vernacular Liberian English incl. Soldier/Firestone English, and Liberian Settler English = 'Congo English', the L1 of Americo-Liberian descendants, studied by Singler in Sinoe County) under this code; no separate glottocodes for LibSE or VLE were found. The quoted statement comes from the Liberian Settler English phonology chapter and characterises LibSE against 'all other Liberian varieties of English' (VLE explicitly; KPE by the chapter's own taxonomy in §1.1). Singler 1981 (open, saved) describes mainly Vernacular Liberian English of Monrovia and calls KPE a subtype of 'Liberian Pidgin English'. Nothing opened describes Kru Pidgin English prosody on its own; that would be Singler 1990: 229.
